ref: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 2.9.7 (Whiston transl.; Book II ch. 9 sec. 7)
quote_en: Thermuthis therefore perceiving him to be so remarkable a child, adopted him for her son, having no child of her own. And when one time had carried Moses to her father, she showed him to him, and said she thought to make him her successor, if it should please God she should have no legitimate child of her own; and to him, "I have brought up a child who is of a divine form, and of a generous mind; and as I have received him from the bounty of the river, in, I thought proper to adopt him my son, and the heir of thy kingdom."
licence_note: Whiston (1737), Project Gutenberg #2848 (US public domain). Footnote marker '21' inside the speech removed. Greek original not read.
from_: Thermuthis therefore perceiving him to be
keys: adopted him for her son
having no child of her own
adopt him my son, and the heir of thy kingdom
what_it_shows: Josephus says Pharaoh's daughter (named Thermuthis) 'adopted him for her son' and proposes to make him 'the heir of thy kingdom'. In the text the adoption is linked to her having no legitimate child.
context: Josephus retells the Exodus; Moses is adopted by the princess and shown to Pharaoh. In the same chapter, just before this section, Josephus traces Moses' natural descent: 'Moses was the son of Amram, who was the son of Caath, whose father Levi was the son of Jacob.'
limits: (1) The adopter is an Egyptian princess in a narrative; the statement is Josephus's retelling, not a Jewish legal text. (2) The adoption is conditional in the text: 'if it should please God she should have no legitimate child'. (3) Josephus gives Moses' natural descent from Levi (through Amram) just before the adoption and does not say the adoption changed his tribe or priestly line. (4) The passage speaks of royal succession, not of tribe.

quote_orig: וַיִּגְדַּ֣ל הַיֶּ֗לֶד וַתְּבִאֵ֙הוּ֙ לְבַת־פַּרְעֹ֔ה וַֽיְהִי־לָ֖הּ לְבֵ֑ן וַתִּקְרָ֤א שְׁמוֹ֙ מֹשֶׁ֔ה וַתֹּ֕אמֶר כִּ֥י מִן־הַמַּ֖יִם מְשִׁיתִֽהוּ׃

licence_note: KJV (public domain), Project Gutenberg #10; Hebrew as displayed on Sefaria (vocalized).

what_it_shows: Scripture says that the child 'became her son' to Pharaoh's daughter and that she named him Moses. The verse uses 'son' for the adopted child and gives her the naming. It says nothing about inheritance or tribe.
context: Exod 2:1-2 gives the natural parents first: 'there went a man of the house of Levi, and took to wife a daughter of Levi'. The adoption follows in 2:5-10.
limits: (1) Exod 2:1 (KJV) gives Moses' natural parents as Levites; the verse does not say the adoption changed his tribe. (2) The verse does not mention inheritance. (3) The Gemara (Megilla 13a, see P07) reads 'bore' as credit and says the adoptive woman 'only reared him', so the rabbis did not read the verb literally.

ref: Yevamot 24a (Gemara on Deut 25:6; the levirate firstborn 'shall rise in the name of his brother'; analogy to Gen 48:6)
quote_orig: אתה אומר לנחלה או אינו אלא לשם יוסף קורין אותו יוסף יוחנן קורין אותו יוחנן נאמר כאן יקום על שם אחיו ונאמר להלן (בראשית מח, ו) על שם אחיהם יקראו בנחלתם מה שם האמור להלן נחלה אף שם האמור כאן לנחלה
orig_url: https://www.sefaria.org/api/texts/Yevamot.24a?vhe=Wikisource%20Talmud%20Bavli&context=0 (segment [5]; segment [4] gives Deut 25:6 'יקום על שם אחיו לנחלה')
own_translation_en: Baraita: 'And the firstborn that she bears shall rise in the name of his brother who is dead' (Deut 25:6), for inheritance (lenachalah). Do you say it is for inheritance, or only for the name, as one calls him Joseph and one calls him Yohanan? Here it says 'shall rise in the name of his brother', and there (Gen 48:6) it says 'they shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance'. Just as the name mentioned there is for inheritance, so the name mentioned here is for inheritance.
licence_note: Hebrew: Wikisource (CC-BY-SA per Sefaria; Vilna text PD). English: team translation (no PD English read).
from_: אתה אומר לנחלה או אינו אלא

על שם אחיהם יקראו בנחלתם
אף שם האמור כאן לנחלה
what_it_shows: The Gemara states that the levirate firstborn 'shall rise in the name of his brother' and that the name carries inheritance (lenachalah), by a verbal analogy to Gen 48:6. Law thus assigns a dead man's name and inheritance to a child born after his death to the widow.
context: Mishnah Yevamot (segment [3]): the mitzvah of levirate belongs to the older brother. Gemara [4]: Deut 25:6 read as 'for inheritance'. Gemara [5]: the analogy. Rava in [7] then explains the derivation further.
limits: (1) Rava [7] (own translation): 'Although in the whole Torah no verse departs from its plain sense, here a verbal analogy (gezera shava) has taken it out of its plain sense entirely.' The inheritance reading is therefore a derived, non-plain reading. (2) [8]: without the analogy one would have said 'the name' means a literal name. (3) [12]: 'inheritance depends on the father and not on the mother' (the Gemara's own principle, used to limit the rule). (4) The passage deals with name and inheritance only; it does not mention tribe or priesthood. (5) JE (see P14) says that Bab. Yeb. 24a is where 'this primitive view is no longer accepted'; I did not identify which view JE means, so that claim is UNVERIFIED here. (6) The levirate child is born to the widow, so the 'name' is a legal fiction, not a blood relation to the dead man.

ref: Sanhedrin 19b (Gemara on 2 Sam 21:8: 'the five sons of Michal ... whom she bore to Adriel'; R. Yehoshua ben Korḥa)
quote_orig: ור' יהושע בן קרחה נמי הכתיב את חמשת בני מיכל בת שאול אמר לך רבי יהושע וכי מיכל ילדה והלא מירב ילדה מירב ילדה ומיכל גידלה לפיכך נקראו על שמה ללמדך שכל המגדל יתום בתוך ביתו מעלה עליו הכתוב כאילו ילדו
quote_en: Did, then, Michal bear them? Was it not Merab who bore them, whereas Michal merely brought them up? But they bore the name of Michal, because the Scripture considers the one who brings up an orphan as if it were born to him.
licence_note: Rodkinson (1918, public domain); OCR spacing and punctuation normalized ('bore them ?' to 'bore them?'); line-break hyphen 'Mi-chal' joined. Hebrew: Wikisource (CC-BY-SA per Sefaria metadata; Vilna text PD).
to: if it were born to him.
keys: Was it not Merab who bore them
they bore the name of Michal
as if it were born to him
what_it_shows: The Gemara asks how the five sons can be called Michal's when Merab bore them, and answers that they were named after Michal because she raised them. It states that anyone who raises an orphan in his house is credited by Scripture 'as if he had given birth' to him. The Gemara ties this credit to the children being called by her name.
context: Sanhedrin 19b, in the discussion of whether David married Merab or Michal (2 Sam 21:8; 1 Sam 25:44; 2 Sam 3:14). The passage is a Scripture-based derivation (aggadah), not a legal ruling. Ruth 4:17 (Ruth bore, Naomi reared), Ps 77:16 and Num 3:1 follow in the same passage.
limits: (1) The text credits the children's name ('they were called by her name'); it does not say the children became Michal's heirs or changed their tribe, and Merab is kept as the birth-mother ('Was it not Merab who bore them'). (2) It is an exegetical derivation explaining a naming, not a legal rule of adoption. (3) The phrase Scripture uses is 'ascribes credit' (maaleh alav ha-katuv), an ascription, not a legal status. (4) JE (P14) calls this the doctrine that the rearer 'is deemed its parent', but JE also says formal adoption is unknown to biblical and Talmudic law; the team should weigh both. (5) Sefaria's Rashi on Sanh 19b has only three segments (opening), and none comments on the Michal clause; no Rashi on this clause was found.

quote_orig: וַיַּ֤רְא יוֹסֵף֙ לְאֶפְרַ֔יִם בְּנֵ֖י שִׁלֵּשִׁ֑ים גַּ֗ם בְּנֵ֤י מָכִיר֙ בֶּן־מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה יֻלְּד֖וּ עַל־בִּרְכֵּ֥י יוֹסֵֽף׃
quote_en: And Joseph saw Ephraim’s children of the third generation: the children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph’s knees.
licence_note: KJV (public domain), Project Gutenberg #10. The Hebrew verb is 'yulledu' (were born); KJV renders 'brought up'.
from_: children also of Machir the son of
keys: children also of Machir the son of Manasseh
upon Joseph’s knees
בְּנֵ֤י מָכִיר֙ בֶּן־מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה
עַל־בִּרְכֵּ֥י יוֹסֵֽף
what_it_shows: The verse says that the children of Machir, son of Manasseh, were born (Hebrew yulledu) 'upon Joseph's knees' (KJV: 'brought up'). The knee formula counts these great-grandchildren to Joseph, while the verse names them by their father Machir.
context: Gen 50:22-23 closes the Joseph cycle: Joseph sees Ephraim's grandchildren and Machir's children (Manasseh's line).
limits: (1) The verse keeps the children under their natural father, 'Machir the son of Manasseh'; it does not say the knee-formula changed their tribe or line. (2) It describes no legal procedure for adoption. (3) The KJV rendering 'brought up' differs from the Hebrew verb 'born' (yalad, passive yulledu); the 'born on the knees' reading is the one the Hebrew supports. (4) JE (P14) cites this verse as one example of the knee-mode of adoption; that is JE's reading.

ref: Genesis 30:3-6; Genesis 35:25 (with Rashi on 30:3, W09, and Bereshit Rabbah 71:7, W12)

quote_en: And she said, Behold my maid Bilhah, go in unto her; and she shall bear upon my knees, that I may also have children by her.
licence_note: KJV (public domain), Project Gutenberg #10. Hebrew via Sefaria. Gen 35:25 KJV: 'And the sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s handmaid; Dan, and Naphtali.' Rashi (Rosenbaum & Silbermann, public domain) and Bereshit Rabbah 71:7 (Sefaria, CC-BY) also read (see limits).

that I may also have children by her
וְתֵלֵד֙ עַל־בִּרְכַּ֔י
what_it_shows: Rachel gives her maid Bilhah to Jacob so that the child will be born 'upon my knees' and Rachel 'may also have children'. Scripture then names Dan and Naphtali as 'the sons of Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid' (Gen 35:25), which ties them to Bilhah and to Jacob, not to Rachel by birth.
context: Gen 30:1-8: Rachel is barren, gives Bilhah; Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali; Rachel names Dan (30:6). Gen 35:25 lists the maid's sons among Jacob's sons. (Whether Dan and Naphtali are counted among the twelve tribes via Jacob is not checked here.)
limits: (1) Gen 35:25 calls them 'the sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s handmaid', not Rachel's sons. (2) Rashi on Gen 30:3 (public domain, W09): 'UPON MY KNEES — as the Targum takes it: she will bear children and I will rear them.' Rashi reads the knees as rearing, not birth. (3) Bereshit Rabbah 71:7 (CC-BY, W12): 'just as that one was built through her rival wife, this one too was built through her rival wife' — a figurative building (credit), not a stated legal transfer. (4) JE (P14) cites Gen 30:3 as evidence of a knee-mode of adoption; that is JE's reading.

ref: Megillah 13a (Gemara on 1 Chr 4:18 and Exod 2:5-10: Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter, 'bore' Jered etc.)
quote_orig: ילדה והא רבויי רביתיה לומר לך שכל המגדל יתום ויתומה בתוך ביתו מעלה עליו הכתוב כאילו ילדו
quote_en: Did she bear him — she only reared him? From this we may infer that whoso rears an orphan is the same as if she bore him.
licence_note: Rodkinson vol. 8 (1918, public domain), OCR. Hebrew: Wikisource (CC-BY-SA per Sefaria metadata; Vilna text PD).

what_it_shows: On 1 Chr 4:18 the Gemara asks whether Pharaoh's daughter 'bore' Moses or only 'reared' him, and states the general principle that whoever rears an orphan boy or girl in his house is credited by Scripture 'as if he gave birth to him'. The principle concerns the credit given by the verse, not a legal status.
context: Megillah 13a opens the Gemara on the Book of Esther via 1 Chr 4:18, Exod 2:5 and Pharaoh's daughter. Segments [12]-[13] then discuss Esther 2:7 ('Mordecai took her to him as a daughter').
limits: (1) The principle is stated as a derivation from a verse about names; it is not a legal rule about adoption, lineage, tribe or inheritance. (2) The same chapter contradicts an adoptive reading of Esther: the baraita of R. Meir (Megilla 13a [13], team translation): 'Do not read le-bat (for a daughter) but le-bayit (for a house)', and this indicates that Mordecai took Esther to be his wife; the Gemara then supports it with II Sam 12:3 (the ewe lamb 'as a daughter' = 'as a house'). The Rodkinson text does not include this baraita. (3) JE (P14) says no method for making Esther Mordecai's heiress is known to Israel's laws. (4) The Gemara's word is 'rearing', not 'begetting', for Pharaoh's daughter.

ref: Sanhedrin 19b (R. Shmuel b. Naḥmani in the name of R. Yonatan on Num 3:1-2: Aaron and Moses)
quote_orig: כל המלמד בן חבירו תורה מעלה עליו הכתוב כאילו ילדו שנאמר (במדבר ג, א) ואלה תולדות אהרן ומשה וכתיב ואלה שמות בני אהרן לומר לך אהרן ילד ומשה לימד לפיכך נקראו על שמו
quote_en: He who teaches the Torah to the son of his neighbor, the Scripture considers him as if he were born to him. As it is written [Num. iii. 1]: “And these are the generations of Aaron and Moses”; and the following verse reads: “And these are the names of the sons of Aaron.” It is only to say that they were born to Aaron and Moses taught them, and therefore they were named after him.
licence_note: Rodkinson vol. 15 (1918, public domain), p. 50; OCR: 'iii. i' written as 'iii. 1' and the doubled full stop at the end removed. Hebrew: Wikisource (CC-BY-SA per Sefaria; Vilna PD).

Aaron and Moses taught them

what_it_shows: The Gemara says that Scripture credits a man who teaches another's son Torah 'as if he had begotten him'. It explains that Aaron's sons are listed under Moses' name because Aaron 'begat' them and Moses 'taught' them.
context: Sanhedrin 19b, the last of the three derivations (after Michal/Merab, Ruth 4:17, Ps 77:16). Scripture derivation again, not a ruling.
limits: (1) The Gemara keeps Aaron as the begetter ('Aaron begat them', 'ahron yalad') and gives Moses only teaching and naming credit. (2) Only naming ('named after him') is stated as an effect; no inheritance or tribe is mentioned. (3) It is an exegetical derivation (aggadah), not a legal ruling on adoption.

quote_en: “She named him Moses” – from here you learn the reward of those who perform of acts of kindness. Although Moses had many names, the name that was set for him throughout the Torah was only the one that Batya daughter of Pharaoh called him.
licence_note: The Sefaria Midrash Rabbah, 2022 (English): CC-BY (Sefaria metadata). Hebrew 'TE' licence unknown (not quoted).

what_it_shows: The midrash says Pharaoh's daughter 'named him Moses' and that the name Moses that stands throughout the Torah is the one she gave. Earlier in the same passage she treats him 'as though he were her son'.
context: Shemot Rabbah 1:26 expands Exod 2:10 (a long midrash on Pharaoh's daughter's love for the child and the magicians' test).
limits: (1) This is midrash ('as though he were her son'); it gives no legal basis for lineage, tribe or inheritance. (2) The brief's claim that this passage carries the 1 Chr 4:18 'daughter of God' line is NOT borne out: the text contains neither 'Chronicles' nor 'daughter of God' (checked). (3) The name 'Batya' is the midrash's own name for the princess.

ref: Kiddushin 70b (Shmuel in the name of ... on Pashhur ben Immer's slaves; priestly status)
quote_orig: אמר רב יהודה אמר שמואל ארבע מאות עבדים ואמרי לה ארבעת אלפים עבדים היו לו לפשחור בן אימר וכולם נטמעו בכהונה וכל כהן שיש בו עזות פנים אינו אלא מהם
own_translation_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: 400 slaves, and some say 4,000 slaves, belonged to Pashhur ben Immer, and they were all absorbed into the priesthood (nitma'u bekhehunah); any priest with insolence is only from them.
licence_note: Hebrew: Wikisource (CC-BY-SA per Sefaria; Vilna PD). English: team translation (no PD English read).
from_: אמר רב יהודה אמר שמואל ארבע מאות עבדים

ארבע מאות עבדים

what_it_shows: The Gemara reports Shmuel's claim that the slaves of a priest (Pashhur ben Immer) were 'absorbed into the priesthood' and that insolent priests descend from them. The text presents household incorporation as a route into priestly standing, but as a contested claim about slave origins.
context: Kiddushin 70b, in a discussion of flawed lineage (slave descent, ḥalalim, mamzerim). Just before, Rav Yehuda proclaims some families in Pumbedita to be of slave descent, and Rav Yosef says the residents of Bei Kuvei are all descendants of slaves.
limits: (1) Rabbi Elazar disagrees in the same passage: 'if you see an insolent priest, do not speculate about him' (that he may be of flawed lineage), citing Hos 4:4. Abaye remarks that they 'all sit in the row in Neharde'a' and that this disagrees with R. Elazar (team translation). (2) The same passage treats slave-descent as a flaw in lineage, the opposite of honour. (3) The text does not describe an adoption procedure; 'absorbed' is the Talmud's word. (4) Claim is attributed to Shmuel by Rav Yehuda; it is a tradition, not a legal ruling.

ref: Bava Batra 109b (Gemara on the Torah's 'family' for inheritance, Num 27:8-11)
quote_orig: אמר רבא אמר קרא ממשפחתו וירש אותה משפחת אב קרויה משפחה משפחת אם אינה קרויה משפחה דכתיב למשפחותם לבית אבותם
quote_en: Said Rabha: It is written [xxvi. 11] "next to him of his family," and the family is named only from the father's side as [ibid., 2] "after their families, by the descent from their fathers."
licence_note: Rodkinson vol. 14 (1918, public domain), p. 243-244, OCR. OCR fixes: '[xxvi. 1 1]' read as '[xxvi. 11]', 'ofrhis' read as 'of his', '.named' read as 'named'. Hebrew: Wikisource (CC-BY-SA per Sefaria; Vilna PD).

keys: named only from the father's side
by the descent from their fathers
משפחת אם אינה קרויה משפחה
what_it_shows: Rava (Rabha) concludes from Num 27:11 and Num 1:2 that 'the family' of a man is his father's family ('משפחת אב קרויה משפחה'), and that his mother's family is 'not called family'.
context: Bava Batra 109b, on the inheritance order (Num 27:8-11): does a father precede the daughter? Is 'his kinsman' the father or the mother? Rava settles the question of 'family' by the father's side.
limits: (1) The rule concerns the Torah's inheritance terms ('family' in Num 27:11); it does not discuss adopted or legally reckoned children. (2) The Gemara raises an immediate counter-verse (Judges 17:7, a Levite 'of the family of Judah'), resolved in P12. (3) The rule places a man's family on the father's side, which is consistent with the Mishnah's lineage rule (P13). It does not support a claim that mother or upbringing alone defines family. (4) Whether a legal father's family counts as the father's family is not addressed in this passage.

ref: Bava Batra 109b (Gemara on Judges 17:7 and 18:30; 1 Chr 23:15: the Levite 'of the family of Judah')
quote_orig: אלא מתוך שעשה מעשה מנשה תלאו הכתוב במנשה הכא נמי מתוך שעשה מעשה מנשה דאתי מיהודה תלאו הכתוב ביהודה
quote_en: It is written Menashe, because he acted like Menashe, who was an idolator; and therefore the phrase "of Judah" is employed because Menashe came from Judah.
licence_note: Rodkinson vol. 14 (1918, public domain), p. 244, OCR. Hebrew: Wikisource (CC-BY-SA per Sefaria; Vilna PD). Quotation marks normalized: the OCR prints " of Judah " with spaces inside the quotation marks; the words are unchanged.

is employed because Menashe came from Judah

what_it_shows: The Gemara explains that the verse calls the Levite 'of the family of Judah' because he acted like Manasseh (who came from Judah). So a family name can be ascribed by conduct, while the man is in fact a Levite through his father. The same passage identifies Jonathan (Judges 18:30) as Moses' son, called 'son of Manasseh' by the verse.
context: Bava Batra 109b, after P11. Judges 17:7 (KJV): 'a young man out of Bethlehem-judah of the family of Judah, who was a Levite'. The Gemara's first answer (his name was Levi) is rejected via Judges 18:30 and 1 Chr 23:15 ('The sons of Moses were, Gershom, and Eliezer').
limits: (1) The Gemara first offers 'his name was Levi' (Rava bar Rav Ḥanan's first answer), then rejects it; the final answer is conduct-based ascription. (2) The verse 'linked him to Judah' while he was a Levite: the Talmud keeps the father's tribe and treats the verse's ascription as moral labelling, not as a tribal transfer. (3) R. Yoḥanan (in the name of R. Shimon b. Yoḥai) says 'we confer a corrupt name on a corrupt man' (Rodkinson), i.e. ascription is punitive. (4) No discussion of adoption in the passage.

ref: Kiddushin 66b, Mishnah on lineage (segments [13] and [15]) and the Gemara that follows at [16]
quote_orig: כל מקום שיש קידושין ואין עבירה הולד הולך אחר הזכר ואיזה זו זו כהנת לויה וישראלית שנשאו לכהן לוי וישראל וכל מי שאין לה לא עליו ולא על אחרים קידושין הולד כמותה ואיזה זה זה ולד שפחה ונכרית
own_translation_en: Wherever there is kiddushin (valid betrothal) and no transgression, the child follows the male; and which is this? The priest's daughter, the Levite's daughter, or the Israelite woman who married a priest, a Levite, or an Israelite. And whenever a woman cannot be betrothed to him or to others, the child is like her; and which is this? The child of a maidservant or of a gentile woman.
licence_note: Hebrew: Wikisource (CC-BY-SA per Sefaria; Vilna PD). English: team translation (no PD English read).

ולד שפחה ונכרית
what_it_shows: The Mishnah states that where a valid marriage takes place without transgression, the child follows the male (father); where the woman could not marry the man, 'the child is like her', as for the child of a maidservant or a gentile woman. Lineage is fixed by the parents' marriage status, and the Mishnah does not mention adoption or upbringing.
context: Mishnah Kiddushin ch. 3 as printed at Kiddushin 66b. The Gemara begins at [16] with R. Shimon's objection: is it an established principle that the child follows the male wherever there is betrothal without transgression?
limits: (1) Gemara [16] tests the general rule (R. Shimon's objection); I did not translate the continuation. (2) The rule covers children of marriages and of barred women; it does not address adoption or fostering, and 'the child is like her' places a child 'not his father's son' in the mother's status. (3) The rule supports the father-line emphasis, but the Mishnah ties it to a valid marriage, not to upbringing.

ref: Jewish Encyclopedia, art. 'Adoption' (Dembitz and Kohler), section 'Adoption in Female Line'
quote_en: The adrogatio of the older Roman law—a legal process by which a man can create betweenhimself and a person not his child relations that properly belong only to father and child—is unknown to both Biblical and Talmudic law.
licence_note: Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906), public domain by date. The source text has the typo 'betweenhimself' (kept as printed). Commentator article.
from_: The adrogatio of the older Roman law
keys: relations that properly belong only to father and child
is unknown to both Biblical and Talmudic law
what_it_shows: JE states that the Roman adrogatio (legal adoption creating father-child relations) is unknown to biblical and Talmudic law, but that the Talmud (Sanh. 19b) honours the rearer as parent. JE also says the knee-formula appears in Gen 30:3 and that Gen 48:5 probably reflects adoption 'in the legal sense'.
context: JE (1901-1906) by Lewis N. Dembitz and Kaufmann Kohler; it discusses Sanh. 19b, Ruth 4:17, Ps 77:16, Num 3, Moses/Bithiah, Esther 2:7, Gen 48:5, Gen 30:3 and the levirate (Yev. 24a).
limits: (1) JE: 'neither does it appear that a method for creating such a relation between them as would make her his heiress was ever known to the laws of Israel' (on Esther). (2) JE says Gen 48:5 'probably' shows adoption 'in the legal sense' with inheritance; that is JE's inference from the verse, not the verse's statement. (3) JE: 'Adoption in the Roman sense did not exist among the ancient Hebrews' (from the levirate). (4) JE refers to 'Bab. Yeb. 24a, where this primitive view is no longer accepted' without naming the view; not verified here (see P03).

ref: CCAR Responsum 63, 'Adoption and Adopted Children' (1978), ARR 203-207

licence_note: CCAR responsum (1978), on-page licence not stated; in copyright; one fragment quoted (under 60 words). Not a halakhic authority for Orthodox law; a modern Reform answer. Quote is 15 words, shorter than the 25-word minimum, because of the one-fragment rule for in-copyright texts.

Aaronite priesthood
what_it_shows: A 1978 Reform responsum says that a child of parents who could lawfully marry under Jewish law is Jewish and may be adopted, 'except that the child could not share in the traditional privileges of the Aaronite priesthood'. It also says the legal section of the Talmud contains nothing about adoption and that the agadot about Moses and Naomi 'are not halachic statements'.
context: Question from Rabbi Michael M. Remson (Family Life Committee). The answer reviews Meg. 13a and San. 19b, Exodus Rabbah 45 and Isaiah 64:8, then gives practical guidance (naming, conversion, ritual).
limits: (1) The responsum says the agadot in Meg. 13a and San. 19b are 'not halachic statements' but 'indicate a climate of opinion which definitely favored adoption'. (2) It is a modern Reform responsum, and the priesthood limit is its own ruling; it is not a classical source. (3) I read the responsum but did not check Exodus Rabbah 45 or Isaiah 64:8 directly.
